items.prompt: What is the passage mainly about?
options: Why seawater prevents grasses from growing
Why limiting visitors is the main requirement for conserving a salt marsh

How marsh growth and surrounding conditions influence marsh survival
items.explanation: The passage connects marsh growth with conditions needed for its survival.
items.title: The slow work of a salt marsh
items.passage:
A salt marsh is a coastal area where grasses grow in ground that is regularly covered by seawater. Although a marsh may look like an unchanging field, its surface is being built and reshaped. As the tide moves through the grasses, the stems slow the water. Some of the fine material carried by that water settles instead of being swept away. Dead roots and leaves also add material to the soil.
These processes can gradually raise the marsh surface. This matters because marsh plants cannot survive indefinitely under deep water. When the land gains height at a rate close to the rise in local water level, the plants may remain within a suitable range of flooding. However, an increase in sediment is not automatically enough to protect every marsh. The supply of material, the health of the plants, and room for the marsh to spread inland all influence the outcome.
For coastal planners, protecting a marsh therefore involves more than preventing people from walking on its grasses. A wall or road behind the marsh may block its inland movement. Measures that protect a single present-day boundary can, in this way, limit the space that the living system will need later.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea?
options: An address system can rely on shared records without changes to residents’ habits
Addresses work through shared systems as well as physical labels
Delivery organizations need separate address systems
Keeping older place names in use prevents a standardized address system from functioning
items.explanation: The passage stresses the coordinated system behind an address.
items.title: Addresses and delivery networks
items.passage:
An address seems to describe a location, but a working address also belongs to a communication system. A house can be familiar to its neighbors and still be difficult for an outside delivery service to find. Descriptions such as “behind the old mill” may work locally, yet become uncertain when a landmark disappears or several places share similar features.
Standardized street names and building numbers reduce this dependence on local knowledge. Their usefulness increases when many organizations use the same system. A supplier, a postal worker, and an emergency service can then interpret the same destination without negotiating a new description. The address acts as a shared reference, even though each organization has a different purpose.
Introducing such a system is not simply a matter of putting numbers on doors. Records must be updated, residents must learn the new descriptions, and older names may continue to circulate. During the transition, keeping a link between old and new descriptions can prevent confusion. This is especially important where the older names carry social or historical significance.
The history of addressing thus illustrates a broader point about infrastructure. A physical sign is only one visible part of a network that depends on compatible records and shared habits of interpretation.

items.prompt: Why are students asked to vote before discussion?
options: To select which partner they will work with
To avoid answering any additional questions
To decide whether the class should use technology
To reveal their initial understanding
items.explanation: The first vote establishes a starting point.
items.title: Learning from an anonymous vote
items.passage:
In a large class, an instructor cannot easily tell whether silence means understanding or uncertainty. One way to gather more information is to ask students to answer a conceptual question anonymously before discussing it with a partner. The class then votes again. The first vote gives the instructor a starting point; the second shows whether explanations exchanged by students have changed their judgments.
An increase in correct answers may be encouraging, but it needs careful interpretation. Some students may simply adopt a confident partner’s choice without understanding the reasoning. To distinguish agreement from learning, an instructor can ask a related question that uses a different example. Success on this new question provides stronger evidence that students can apply an idea rather than repeat an answer.
The quality of the original question also matters. If it can be answered by recalling a word, there may be little to discuss. A useful question instead presents alternatives that reflect different ways of thinking about the same situation. Students then need to explain why one account works better than another.
Anonymous voting is therefore not valuable merely because it introduces technology into a classroom. Its value depends on how the sequence of voting, explanation, and further questioning makes students’ reasoning visible.

items.prompt: What is the talk mainly explaining?
options: Why heating systems should run continuously
How feedback can help maintain a stable condition
How room size determines the cost of electricity
Why negative feedback damages household devices
items.explanation: The thermostat illustrates active correction toward a target.
items.title: Feedback and a room thermostat

stimulus.title: Feedback and a room thermostat
stimulus.script:
Let’s use a familiar device to understand negative feedback: a room thermostat. You choose a temperature, and the thermostat compares that setting with the temperature it measures. If the room is too cold, it signals the heating system to run. As the room warms, the difference becomes smaller, and eventually the heating stops. The word negative doesn’t mean that the process is harmful. It means that the response works against the original difference.
Now, there’s usually a delay between switching on the heater and warming the whole room. A sensor beside the heater may report warmth before someone at the far end of the room feels it. So the position of the sensor matters, as does the time the system takes to respond. A system that reacts too strongly to every small difference can keep overshooting its target, then correcting in the opposite direction.
This is why a useful control system doesn’t simply demand the fastest possible response. It needs an appropriate response to a reliable measurement. The thermostat example helps us see a general principle: maintaining a stable condition is often an active process. The system keeps making adjustments even when, from our point of view, very little seems to be changing.

items.prompt: What does “negative” mean in this context?
options: The measured temperature is below zero
The effect of the device is harmful
The response opposes a difference from the target
The heating system has failed to operate
items.explanation: The response counteracts the initial deviation.

items.prompt: What is the speaker’s main point?
options: Every replica should look identical to its original in all respects
A replica is useful only when the original has been lost
A replica’s educational value depends on its purpose and clear labeling
Visitors learn more from replicas than from original objects
items.explanation: The talk links selected reproduced properties with an educational goal.
items.title: Making a museum replica useful

stimulus.title: Making a museum replica useful
stimulus.script:
When you see a replica in a museum, you might think it’s there because the original object was unavailable. Sometimes that’s true. But a replica can also allow an experience that the original cannot safely provide. Visitors might handle a copy of a carved tool, for example, and feel where its maker placed the grip. Repeated handling could damage the original, so the copy makes a particular kind of learning possible.
The challenge is deciding what the replica needs to reproduce. If the question concerns how a tool was held, its weight and surface may matter. If the purpose is to explain the order in which its parts were assembled, a transparent section might be more useful than a perfectly matched color. Accuracy is therefore related to the question the replica is being used to explore.
That doesn’t mean museums can ignore differences. A visitor needs to know that an object is a replica and which features have been changed. Otherwise, an educational modification may be mistaken for evidence about the original.
So a good replica is neither a failed original nor simply a convincing imitation. It’s a tool for directing attention. By making some properties available for examination, it can support understanding, provided that its limitations remain clear.

items.prompt: What is the main topic?
options: How compost piles can operate without living organisms
How plant remains can be stored without decomposition
Why woody material should be removed from every compost pile
Why effective composting requires attention to changing conditions
items.explanation: The talk emphasizes diagnosing conditions for decomposition.
items.title: What compost needs

stimulus.title: What compost needs
stimulus.script:
A compost pile transforms plant remains through the activity of living organisms. It isn’t simply a heap that becomes useful if you leave it alone for long enough. The organisms breaking down the material need suitable conditions, including moisture and access to air. When the pile is very wet and compacted, air moves through it less easily, and the process can change.
One practical response is to mix materials with different structures. Soft, wet vegetable remains may pack tightly together. Drier stalks or small pieces of woody material can help create spaces within the mixture. Those spaces matter because they allow air to reach more of the material. Turning the pile can also redistribute material and reopen spaces that have collapsed.
However, turning more often isn’t automatically better. A pile that is too dry may need moisture rather than another round of mixing. The useful action depends on what is limiting the process at that moment.
Think of composting as managing relationships among materials and organisms. A single sign, such as slow change, can have more than one explanation. Before choosing a remedy, you need to look at the conditions. This is a small-scale example of a broader approach in environmental work: diagnose the cause, rather than applying the same treatment whenever an outcome looks similar.

They make the whole pile more compact
items.explanation: Their structure can preserve air spaces.

Drier stalks or small pieces of woody material can help create spaces within the mixture. Those spaces matter because they allow air to reach more of the material. Turning the pile can also redistribute material and reopen spaces that have collapsed.
However, turning more often isn’t automatically better. A pile that is too dry may need moisture rather than another round of mixing. The useful action depends on what is limiting the process at that moment.
Think of composting as managing relationships among materials and organisms. A single sign, such as slow change, can have more than one explanation. Before choosing a remedy, you need to look at the conditions. This is a small-scale example of a broader approach in environmental work: diagnose the cause, rather than applying the same treatment whenever an outcome looks similar.

The workshop can still take place if the item is supplied or a suitable alternative is arranged. Write to the equipment coordinator.
points: Identify your booking and explain what is missing.
Explain how the missing item affects the planned workshop.
Request a practical solution and say when you are available to collect it.

items.title: Write for an Academic Discussion
items.question: Our class is considering how universities should improve student life with a limited budget. Some people favor extending the hours of existing facilities; others favor creating new activities during normal hours. Which approach should receive priority? Explain how your choice would address a real student need.
students: I would extend opening hours. Many students have classes or jobs during the day, so an excellent facility is not useful to them if it closes before they can get there. Better access could help without constructing another building.

I would add new activities. Longer hours may benefit the same students who already use a facility. New activities could attract people who have not found anything that interests them and help them feel part of the university.
